title: Born 1900, buying a cornet in 1918, Hotsy Totsy jam sessions
summary: Fougerat wanted to be a locomotive engineer, bought a rusty cornet on Rampart Street, taught himself in the key of C, and later played jam sessions at the Hotsy Totsy c.1924.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Well, I was born in New Orleans in 1900, April 25th. And I started my... Funny thing about music, never even had music in my brain. I always wanted to be a locomotive engineer. When I was a kid, I always fooled around engines. And I went along, and here comes around the year 1918. Instead of winding up getting a job in the railroad, I wind up being a musician. In fact, it was just born on me. I never took a lesson. I just bought a horn on Ramport Street. I never will forget that. It was a tin horn. I don't remember the make of it anymore. I didn't know it was a cornet. And the valves was rusty, and I had a wake on it. And I started blowing on that thing in one key. I always did playing a key of C. That was a big deal in them days, playing one key. In fact, in those days, the musicians just played in about two keys, C and F. Put them in another key, and they got lost. But in later years, I've played with musicians like Leonard Beisdorf. It's Johnny Beisdorf's brother. And he played in all black keys, and I didn't even know what it was, because I was only playing in this key of C, because everybody in those days tuned up in the same key. With the piano. Everybody tuned up with the piano, and we all played in the same key. Until I got mingling around in later years, about 1923 or 1924, I got to play with some pretty good musicians, like I said, Leonard Beisdorf, and Leo Addy, and the piano player, the name of Joe Gary, just did. Now, we all played a little job. I played over at the Hotsy Totsy. Then it was about a half a block from Little Club in them days. I don't know if you remember them. Well, I'm telling you, it's way back in 1924, something like that. And we used to play upstairs. This was an upstairs place, and everybody had a regular jam session. Everybody would come around in the morning when they were off, and was a piano player. He's dead now with the name of Lobosky, and Max Fink was a very noted violinist. They all used to come over there in the morning to hear this kind of music, because they were playing all that, what you call long hair music all night, and they used to like to hear this stuff. They didn't know how it came out the horns or anything else. They used to go over there, just loved it, and want to hit, and they used to get there every morning. We used to have a big jam session, and have a big cheese box for a kitty in them days. They used to just throw the money in there to hear us play.
